newsitem.title: PERU: Hostages beg Peru for peaceful end to crisis.
newsitem.headline: Hostages beg Peru for peaceful end to crisis.

text.p: About 340 hostages trapped in the Japanese ambassador's residence begged Peru on Saturday to negotiate a peaceful end to the four-day siege as the Marxist hostage-takers complained about the government's hard line.

The guerrillas released 38 hostages on Friday night into the arms of frantic, weeping relatives, some of whom hurled themselves onto the roofs of ambulances in their desperation to embrace their loved ones.
"My prayers were heard, now we must keep praying for those who are still inside the residence" said Jenny Bumachar, a relative of one of those released.

Victims still in the building on Saturday were suffering from stinking overcrowded toilets, poor food, stifling heat and a lack of room after a fourth night sleeping on the floor in crumpled and smelly suits, Red Cross officials said.
Repeating earlier fruitless appeals, hostages early on Saturday thrust up to an embassy window signs begging the government to allow running water to be reconnected.

To pass the long hours inside, the at least 22 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas organised round table discussions with the captive ambassadors and government officials on political and ideological topics, released hostage Manuel Romero told local media.

Rebels allowed small portable toilets to be taken inside to relieve bathroom overcrowding, Red Cross coordinator Jens Amlie said. The guerrillas had earlier refused to allow toilet cabins to be set up in the grounds of the residence.
Friday's freed captives carried with them two messages: one from the heavily armed MRTA rebels who stormed the residence last Tuesday and one from the hostages.
The guerrillas held out the carrot of "significant" further hostage releases if the government let them speak to their jailed colleagues by telephone.
But they also stood firm on their main demand since the crisis began: the release of all the more than 400 MRTA prisoners in Peruvian jails.

"We ratify the firmness of our requests," the rebel statement said. "Whatever extreme measure that puts at physical risk the jailed people will be the exclusive responsibility of the government." The government attitude so far "does nothing to contribute to a solution," it added.
Released hostages like opposition congressman Javier Diez warned reporters that the situation inside the residence was "bad" and pleaded with the government to negotiate.
But President Alberto Fujimori, closeted with generals and security advisers, gave no sign of relaxing his tough stance.
He has not made any public comment since the crisis broke but did meet a small group of local newspaper editors on Friday to say he had no plans to even talk to the rebels.
"He made it clear that it is not within his plans to negotiate with the subversive group," said the daily Gestion, one of those invited to the private meeting.

Apparently contradicting that statement, Congress president Victor Joy Way said on Saturday in a television interview that the government "had ruled out military action" to end the crisis and was negotiating "serenely and peacefully". He did not mention police action or the use of force in general.
The government has so far rejected all the rebels' demands and deployed more than 900 special police and intelligence agents around the embassy residence.
Anti-terrorism police sources confirmed MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini was inside the residence leading the rebels.
"It's a brave operation. He's playing all his cards with this one," said one source. "So far, he has made a mockery of the Peruvian government, and they won't forgive him for that."

They said there was a growing tide of opinion among the police and military that armed intervention was the only solution. Detailed plans were being drawn up, they added, but the final decision lay with Fujimori.
"We have to enter. There will be a minimum cost but we have to enter," said one anti-terrorism source.
Behind the embassy on Saturday morning, a fleet of 20 ambulances stood with engines running and doctors on board playing cards to pass the time.
"Since the first day we have had orders from the (Interior) minister as to what the plan is," a fire brigade official told Reuters. He would not elaborate.
The sources said Germany, the United States and Britain had all sent security advisers to help Peruvian special forces but no further details were available.
Under international law, Peru must consult Japan before taking any armed action against the residence.
In Milan, two Molotov cocktail firebombs were thrown at the Peruvian consulate early on Saturday by apparent supporters of the MRTA, an Italian police spokesman said.
He said the two bottles exploded but caused little damage and no injury.
